hero.headline: Port St. Lucie leaders to decide how to spend $24 million Waste Pro settlement
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie city officials are working to determine how to allocate the $24 million settlement the city received from its former waste hauler, Waste Pro. City council will address the matter on Monday as it weighs options for distributing funds that resulted from years of service failures during the pandemic. The settlement came after both the city and the company filed lawsuits against each other in 2021. Waste Pro attributed collection problems to labor shortages, while Port St. Lucie argued the company failed to meet contract standards for service quality.

Residents who suffered through the trash collection issues are watching closely as leaders consider their options. Neighbor Kelly Lee, who attended Monday's meeting, witnessed firsthand the problems her neighbors faced. "It would just be a stinky mess on their yard," Lee said. "They didn't pick up, and it's overflowing." Mayor Shannon Martin has indicated her commitment to returning the settlement funds directly to residents. "I'm committed to making sure that our residents get paid back for what they had to deal with during that time," Martin said in April following the settlement announcement.

The distribution of funds raises complicated questions about fairness and eligibility. Some residents who experienced the service failures have since moved away from Port St. Lucie, while new residents arrived after the problems ended. Lee raised these concerns about how former residents should be handled. "People have moved, the residents are no longer here, some of them are brand new residents that didn't pay into waste pro," Lee said. She also questioned where former residents would receive their share if the city decided to distribute payments.

City staff have been preparing recommendations for the council by collecting data and developing different distribution scenarios, according to Scott Samples with the city. "There's a lot of people that have been working on this," Samples said. "Ultimately the goal is to make the best decision possible, help remediate some of those issues, and those nightmares that people have from back then." Residents like Lee hope the process will include community input. "Have us weigh in on something to at least feel part of the process," Lee said. "One size can't fit all."

cards.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier sues TikTok over violations of Florida child social media law
cards.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, alleging the social media platform is violating a 2024 Florida law designed to protect minors online and deceiving parents about the content children access. The complaint centers on House Bill 3, which took effect in January and prohibits children under 14 from creating social media accounts while requiring parental consent for users ages 15 and 16.

Uthmeier stated that TikTok's business model depends on addicting children and teenagers to its platform while knowingly misleading parents. "TikTok knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law," the attorney general said. The lawsuit contends that TikTok misrepresents the types of content available on the platform, downplaying the prevalence of mature themes such as sexual content, drug use, profanity, self-harm and eating disorders despite marketing the app as appropriate for users 13 and older.

Beyond the alleged violations of HB 3, Florida's complaint charges TikTok with engaging in deceptive and unfair trade practices under the state's consumer protection laws by misleading parents about platform safety and content moderation. State attorneys argue that TikTok has long understood the risks its platform poses to young users but continues pursuing growth strategies that target children and teenagers rather than addressing these concerns.

The lawsuit represents a significant enforcement action under Florida's social media law since its implementation earlier this year. The legal challenge reflects a broader national trend of states taking action against social media companies over youth safety concerns. The outcome could establish important precedent for how other states enforce similar restrictions and determine the extent to which social media companies may face liability for allowing underage users or exposing them to inappropriate material. TikTok has not yet responded to the allegations filed in Florida court.

cards.headline: Man dies in Martin County vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard; exhaust ignition suspected
cards.teaser: A man died Saturday night when his truck caught fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court in Martin County, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire that initially appeared to be the result of a crash is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle. The individual was burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives believe they have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed. Those results are expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Martin County Could Lose $67 Million Under Proposed Homestead Exemption Expansion
cards.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could cost Martin County more than $67 million in lost revenue if voters approve the amendment in November, according to analysis from the Florida Policy Institute. The statewide impact would be even more significant, with local governments across Florida potentially losing nearly $4.8 billion under the measure.

The expansion raises concerns about who will ultimately bear the financial burden. Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, says the proposed tax cut would do little for the people his organization serves. He reports seeing an uptick in people seeking help with rent and bills, with 95 percent of those seeking assistance being renters. "The housing situation is so dire," Readling said. "It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday." According to a 2025 Florida Senate analysis, there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters in the state. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said.

Attorney John Tolley explains that local governments facing revenue shortfalls have limited options: cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. If rates rise, landlords who don't receive the homestead exemption could face higher tax bills and potentially pass those costs on to renters. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged this possibility, saying "There could be an effect where we see some people getting priced out of these rentals, which are already pretty high." However, Caputo believes there is a high probability that local municipalities may not raise millage rates at all. He also noted that if landlords do face higher costs, the market may stabilize anyway due to supply and demand dynamics.

The amendment includes another provision that could help offset concerns about rising rents. It would lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent down to 5 percent. Tolley suggested this reduction could potentially lead to lower rents. "The fact that you could have less taxes, you actually might see a trend where rents go down even further than they were before," Tolley said. Caputo added that while landlords may initially try to pass increased costs to tenants, they would have to readjust pricing if demand doesn't support higher rents, since "costs are pretty movable as well."

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million loss from proposed property tax amendment
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders are warning that a proposed property tax amendment could cost the county $50 million in revenue. The warning comes as voters prepare to decide on the amendment in November.

A recent analysis from the Florida Policy Institute estimates that local governments statewide could lose nearly $4.8 billion if voters approve the amendment. The proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption would lower tax bills for homeowners but could force local governments to cut services, use reserves, or raise millage rates to offset the lost revenue.

Critics warn that renters may end up bearing the burden if local governments raise rates. At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling says 95% of the people seeking help with rent and bills are renters. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10% down to 5%. Some analysts believe this could result in lower rents, though others warn landlords facing higher tax bills could pass those costs to tenants. The measure will appear on the November ballot.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach fire kills 4 dogs, exposes animal neglect at 16th Street property
cards.teaser: A fire inside a wooden shed on a West Palm Beach commercial property killed 4 dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals.
cards.body:
Firefighters and police officers arrived at a commercial property in West Palm Beach on Monday morning to find a wooden shed engulfed in flames. The blaze occurred around 7:05 a.m. on the 400 block of 16th Street. When crews extinguished the fire, they discovered the tragic aftermath: four dogs had died in the structure, and another dog had suffered injuries. The animals had been locked inside the shed when the fire started, leaving them unable to escape the dangerous conditions.

The discovery of the deceased and injured animals prompted authorities to conduct a thorough investigation of the entire property. Officers found an additional dog on the premises that had not been harmed by the fire. They also uncovered six cats that were being housed inside a shipping container on the grounds. The investigation revealed the disturbing reality that all of the animals on the property were living in squalid conditions. The inadequate and unsanitary housing for these animals raised serious questions about the care and treatment they had been receiving.

Animal Care and Control intervened immediately, taking custody of all surviving animals discovered at the location. Officials stated that the dogs and cats that survived are expected to make full recoveries from their injuries and trauma. This outcome provided some measure of relief given the deadly nature of the fire and the poor conditions in which the animals had been kept.

The incident also uncovered a history of violations at the property. West Palm Beach Police confirmed that the location had been previously cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations. These prior citations suggest that conditions at the site had been substandard for some time before the Monday morning fire. The investigation into the fire and the circumstances surrounding the animals remains ongoing, with authorities continuing to gather information about how the blaze started and what led to the neglectful housing conditions for the animals on the property.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives repeated toll bills from stolen temporary tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine has received multiple toll bills from roads she never traveled after someone stole her husband's temporary tag and used it on a black Mercedes.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for charges along Florida's Gulf Coast using a temporary tag registered to her husband. The bill showed a black Mercedes, but the Keswicks drive a white Nissan with a permanent tag. After filing a police report with Palm Beach Gardens Police, Keswick-Paine followed their advice and disputed the bill with SunPass rather than paying it. A second invoice arrived despite the dispute, and while SunPass eventually closed the case, Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation the matter was resolved.

Concerned about potential liability, Keswick-Paine reached out to the Florida Department of Transportation in April. The agency acknowledged her questions but never answered them despite multiple follow-up attempts. Since April, she has received a third toll bill. Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said the problem is far more common than many realize. "It's happening a lot," Burnetti said. Security consultant Gene Petrino advised keeping thorough records of police reports and toll disputes, and suggested destroying temporary tags by cutting them into pieces rather than surrendering them with personal information intact.

cards.headline: Big Dog Ranch Rescue secures closure of Wisconsin beagle facility, to relocate 475 dogs to Florida
cards.teaser: Big Dog Ranch Rescue has reached an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin and transfer 475 beagles to its Florida and Alabama campuses.
cards.body:
Big Dog Ranch Rescue has secured an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms, a Wisconsin-based dog breeding and research facility, and transfer all 475 remaining beagles housed there. A total of 325 beagles will be transferred from Ridglan Farms to Big Dog Ranch Rescue today and tomorrow, with the dogs transported to the organization's Florida and Alabama campuses. There, they will receive medical care, including spay and neuter procedures, before being placed for adoption. Some beagles will also be transferred to partner rescue organizations across the country. The remaining 150 dogs are expected to be released to Big Dog Ranch Rescue by the beginning of August, at which point Ridglan Farms will permanently cease its dog breeding, sales, research and testing operations.

Lauree Simmons, founder and CEO of Big Dog Ranch Rescue, thanked Ridglan Farms for coordinating the transfers and committing to close permanently. The agreement follows a large-scale rescue effort carried out on April 29 that resulted in the relocation of 2,110 beagles from the facility. Simmons also thanked Big Dog Ranch Rescue supporters, iPaw Rescue and the Robert and Perri Bishop Foundation for helping make the rescue effort possible. Founded in 2008, Big Dog Ranch Rescue has rescued more than 90,000 dogs and focuses on rescue, rehabilitation, adoption, animal welfare advocacy, disaster response, and spay and neuter initiatives.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, which runs through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is hosting its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge through July 31 under the theme "Unearth a Story." Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win grand prizes.

Prize options vary by age group. Children up to age 4 receive a rubber duck, while kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can select a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events including children's story times, craft sessions, adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances throughout the challenge. The American Library Association notes that summertime reading programs help prevent the "summer slide" in student learning. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach redevelopment projects to bring hundreds of apartments downtown
cards.teaser: Two major redevelopment projects are reshaping downtown Boynton Beach, bringing hundreds of apartments and retail space, but small businesses face an uncertain future.
cards.body:
The Boynton Beach Community Redevelopment Agency is overseeing two major downtown projects: The Villages, which is already under construction, and The Pierce, a proposed development in the permitting process. The Pierce would bring 300 apartments, 17,000 square feet of restaurant, retail, and office space, and 150 public parking spaces. Half of the apartment units will be set aside as workforce housing for at least 15 years, with a portion remaining affordable long-term.

Hurricane Alley, a downtown restaurant owned and operated by Kim Kelly for three decades, stands in the path of The Pierce development. Kelly said she understands the need for redevelopment but wants city leaders to consider what businesses like hers stand to lose. Kelly employs 50 people and said their future is uncertain, with the timeline for any closure remaining unclear. Just a block away, The Villages project is taking shape, bringing 300 apartments, 8,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space, more than 600 parking spots, and a park. Philip Maxwell, a longtime Boynton Beach resident, said he welcomes the development's potential boost to small businesses, though he has concerns about increased traffic and crowds.

cards.headline: Early morning fire kills 4 dogs, exposes animal neglect at West Palm Beach property
cards.teaser: A fire inside a wooden shed on a West Palm Beach property Monday morning killed 4 dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach Fire and Police Departments responded to a fire at a commercial property along the 400 block of 16th Street around 7:05 a.m. Monday. The blaze occurred inside a wooden shed where several dogs were locked inside at the time. The fire killed 4 dogs and injured another.

Further investigation revealed additional animals on the property living in squalid conditions. A dog that was not injured was found on the property, along with 6 cats housed inside a shipping container. Animal Care and Control took custody of the surviving animals, which are expected to recover from their injuries. West Palm Beach Police confirmed the property was cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives toll bills for stolen temporary tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine has received multiple toll bills from Florida's Gulf Coast for a black Mercedes she does not own, linked to a stolen temporary tag registered to her husband.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received her first toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast. The license plate number on the bill matched a temporary tag registered to her husband, but the couple drives a white Nissan that has had a permanent tag for months. The bill referenced a black Mercedes and included a picture of it. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police and did not pay the bill, instead filing a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived anyway. SunPass eventually closed the dispute, but Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation that the matter was resolved. Since reaching out in April, she received a third toll bill. Palm Beach Gardens Police said in an email that they consider the case an isolated incident.

Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said the problem is far more common. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino said the best way to protect yourself from temp tag theft is to keep thorough records of any police reports and toll disputes. Petrino also advised destroying temporary tags by cutting them into pieces or surrendering them to the tag agency with personal information removed. A new law in Florida kicked in last year that increased penalties for the fraudulent use of temp tags and made the tags easier for the state to track.

cards.headline: 14-year-old Boynton Beach boy killed in North Congress Avenue crash
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute of Boynton Beach was struck and killed by a BMW M4 while crossing North Congress Avenue on Friday night.
cards.body:
A 14-year-old Boynton Beach boy was killed Friday night after being struck by a vehicle while crossing North Congress Avenue, according to the Boynton Beach Police Department. The crash happened just before 9 p.m. on June 12 in the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue. Investigators determined that Christopher Cetoute was crossing the roadway in an eastbound direction when he was hit by a BMW M4 traveling southbound. Police said the vehicle appeared to be traveling at a high rate of speed at the time of the crash. Emergency crews from the Boynton Beach Fire Rescue responded to the scene and pronounced Cetoute dead on site.

Officials said all individuals involved remained at the scene following the crash. Authorities have not released additional details about potential charges or contributing factors. The Boynton Beach Police Department is asking anyone with information about the crash to come forward as the case develops. North Congress Avenue was temporarily impacted as investigators processed the scene late Friday night. The investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to reconstruct the circumstances leading up to the collision.

cards.headline: Vanilla Ice surprises Palm Beach County deputy celebrating 30 years of service
cards.teaser: Deputy Tina Izzarone received a surprise visit from rapper Vanilla Ice at a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony, arranged by a young man she had helped during a traffic stop.
cards.body:
Deputy Tina Izzarone was honored at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony this month for 30 years of service. She received an unexpected surprise when her favorite celebrity, rapper Rob Van Winkle, better known as Vanilla Ice, appeared at the event. The surprise was made possible by a young man named Raffie, whose connection to both the deputy and the rapper brought the moment together.

The story began when Izzarone pulled Raffie's mother over for a traffic stop and noticed Raffie. "I noticed immediately of his specialness, and I made him feel really at ease knowing that his mother was not in trouble," Izzarone said. Raffie remembered the deputy's kindness and approached her when they saw each other again a few months later. Raffie also has a longstanding friendship with Van Winkle. When Raffie and his mother planned to attend the awards ceremony, Raffie invited Van Winkle to surprise Izzarone. Van Winkle described his bond with Raffie, saying they go way back since Raffie was a little kid. Adding to the significance of the moment, Van Winkle and Izzarone share the same birthday on October 31. Despite the kindness Izzarone showed that day, Raffie's mother did receive a ticket.

hero.headline: Indian River County leaders warn property tax amendment could cost county $50 million
hero.teaser: Indian River County leaders discussed a property tax amendment heading to the November ballot that could cost the county $50 million in 2028, warning the loss could impact law enforcement and fire rescue services.
hero.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday morning at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss said the state is dictating to local governments how to fund services, while Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called it "unsound, unplanned piece of public policy." According to Lunceford, the county has a budget of around $597 million and could lose approximately $50 million in funding by 2028.

Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of their $70 million budget, with about 79.1% of their funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Brewer warned that three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Lunceford characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut, saying the county could raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties to compensate for lost revenue. He noted that increasing taxes on businesses ultimately increases costs for everyone.

cards.headline: Martin County brush fire contained after burning 105 acres near Palm City Newfield neighborhood
cards.teaser: A 105-acre brush fire near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City is now contained after Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Sheriff's Office worked together to battle the blaze.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office responded to a 105-acre brush fire near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard in the Newfield neighborhood of Palm City. The fire has been contained after multiple agencies worked together to battle the blaze. Residents nearby experienced smoky conditions and increased emergency vehicle activity as crews worked to contain the fire. The smoke and flames were visible from homes in the Newfield neighborhood, drawing crowds of onlookers. Josh Barry, a Newfield resident, said his family was caught off guard when the fire broke out. "My wife just started yelling from upstairs, hey there's a fire outside so I ran up and looked and said wow that's really really close," Barry said. He noted that residents lined up from all over the neighborhood to watch.

Tom Hornbostel, district chief for Martin County Fire Rescue, described how the Division of Forestry and Martin County Sheriff's office helicopter operations helped stop the fire's spread. "With their helicopter drops they were able to go by near lakes, pick up water and do what we call water drops to stop the floor progression of the fire," Hornbostel said. Although some neighbors reported seeing ash fall, fire crews said there was no threat to homes or other structures. Division of Forestry units remained on scene overnight and into Monday morning to monitor for any spot-overs.

cards.headline: Wrongful death suit filed in St. Lucie County Florida Turnpike crash that killed three
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian has filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother Faniola Joseph and two others were killed in a St. Lucie County crash on August 12, 2025, when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were traveling for work in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck's driver, Harjinder Singh of White Hawk Carriers, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three people in the minivan were killed. Joseph, who had been living in Indiana and traveled south to purchase goods for her shop, left behind her only child, Angeline Dowdian, 22, who was living in another country at the time of the crash.

Angeline has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. She is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations. Transportation expert James Lewis described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach fire kills 4 dogs, exposes animal neglect at 16th Street property
cards.teaser: A fire at a West Palm Beach property on Monday morning killed 4 dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals, with all surviving animals now in custody of Animal Care and Control.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach Fire and Police Departments responded to a fire along the 400 block of 16th Street around 7:05 a.m. on Monday morning. The blaze occurred inside a wooden shed on the commercial property, where several dogs were locked inside at the time. The fire killed 4 dogs and injured another dog that was on the property.

Further investigation revealed another uninjured dog on the property, as well as 6 cats housed inside a shipping container. All animals were found living in squalor. Animal Care and Control took custody of the surviving animals, which are expected to recover from their injuries. West Palm Beach Police confirm the property was cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations.

cards.headline: Sara Baxter returns to Palm Beach County Commission race as District 6 candidates respond
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race with President Donald Trump's endorsement, but other candidates say voters need someone committed to the district.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter reentered the District 6 Commission race by meeting the noon qualifying deadline, reversing her earlier decision to run for Congress. She received President Donald Trump's endorsement after Trump asked her to remain in Palm Beach County. Republican candidate Elizabeth Accomando and Democratic candidate Rudolph Tinker both said the issues facing District 6 should outweigh the White House endorsement. Tinker said he thinks Baxter has lost a lot of ground and credibility as a Republican candidate. Accomando said it doesn't make sense to her. Both candidates emphasized that the focus should remain on the community's true needs.

Democratic candidates Katherine Waldron and Mario Guzman also responded to Baxter's reentry. Waldron said running for office is a serious commitment that should not change from one week to the next based on political circumstances or direction from Washington. Guzman said residents of District 6 deserve a candidate committed to public needs who will bring stability. Across all candidates and voters, the main issues facing District 6 are development, traffic, and the emergence of AI data centers. Voters will decide the District 6 race on Primary Day, August 18, with the general election in November.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy surprised by Vanilla Ice at awards ceremony honoring 30 years of service
hero.teaser: Deputy Tina Izzarone received an unexpected visit from rapper Vanilla Ice at the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony this month.
hero.body:
A Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office deputy marking three decades of service received an unexpected gift during an awards ceremony this month when rapper Vanilla Ice made a surprise appearance. Deputy Tina Izzarone was being recognized for her years of dedicated work when Rob Van Winkle, known professionally as Vanilla Ice, walked into the event. The unexpected visit left Izzarone amazed and created a memorable moment she had not anticipated.

The surprise came together through the efforts of a young man named Raffie, who maintained meaningful connections with both the deputy and the rapper. The connection began when Izzarone conducted a traffic stop involving Raffie's mother. During that interaction, Izzarone noticed something special about Raffie and made an effort to put him at ease, making sure he understood his mother was not in trouble. That small gesture of kindness left an impression. When Raffie encountered Izzarone again several months later, he remembered her compassion and approached her to reconnect.

Raffie also shared a long-standing friendship with Van Winkle that stretched back to Raffie's childhood. When Raffie and his mother decided to attend the awards ceremony, Raffie seized the opportunity to invite the rapper to join them. Van Winkle accepted, recognizing Raffie as someone he had known for many years. The rapper spoke about his bond with Raffie, explaining that they spend time together at his home. "I have a big monster truck and every time he comes over and every time he comes to my house he says I have to sit in it," Van Winkle said. "Turns the air conditioner on and it's cool."

The surprise held an additional layer of significance. Van Winkle and Izzarone share the same birthday, October 31, making the encounter even more meaningful. The moment represented more than just celebrity recognition. It demonstrated how a single act of compassion during a routine traffic stop could create a lasting connection and ultimately lead to an unforgettable experience at a professional milestone celebration. Despite the pleasant encounter, Raffie's mother did receive a citation that day.

cards.headline: Martin County vehicle fire kills driver after exhaust ignites grass near Citrus Boulevard
cards.teaser: A fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition rather than a crash.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire that initially appeared to be the result of a crash is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives believe they have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. Due to the condition of the remains, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed, with those results expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach now requires adult chaperones for all guests 17 and under
cards.teaser: South Florida's largest water park has implemented an interim youth supervision policy requiring all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has implemented an interim youth supervision policy requiring all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. According to the park, the policy is part of its ongoing effort to maintain a safe and enjoyable environment for guests at South Florida's largest water park. Minors ages 17 and under must be accompanied by an adult chaperone, defined as a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who is at least 21 years old and traveled to the park with the minor's group.

All adult chaperones must present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry. Chaperones must be present when their group enters the park and remain on-site for the duration of the visit. Rapids Water Park limits each adult chaperone to supervising no more than 5 guests who are 17 years old or younger per day. Park officials said the measure aligns with the park's commitment to providing a family-friendly destination where guests can safely enjoy its attractions. The youth supervision policy is currently listed as an interim measure and is now in effect.

cards.headline: 105-acre brush fire contained near Palm City neighborhood after helicopter water drops
cards.teaser: A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County is now contained after multiple agencies worked together to battle the blaze near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City.
cards.body:
A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County is now contained after multiple agencies responded to the blaze near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City. Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office battled the wildfire near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard. Residents in the area experienced smoky conditions and increased emergency vehicle activity as crews worked to contain the fire. The smoke and flames were visible from homes in the Newfield neighborhood, drawing crowds of onlookers.

Tom Hornbostel, district chief for Martin County Fire Rescue, said the Division of Forestry and Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter operations helped stop the fire's spread by picking up water from nearby lakes and making water drops to slow the progression of the fire. Although some neighbors reported seeing ash fall, fire crews said there was no threat to homes or other structures. Division of Forestry units remained on scene overnight and into Monday morning to closely monitor the fire for any spot-overs. Josh Barry, a Newfield resident who recently moved into the neighborhood, said he was impressed by how quickly crews responded and that the fire was fairly quickly taken care of.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library summer reading challenge offers prizes through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge running through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to "Unearth a Story" this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31. Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen said the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win grand prizes.

The program offers age-specific prizes. Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events including children's story times, craft sessions, adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances. The American Library Association notes that summertime reading programs help prevent the "summer slide" in student learning. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Big Dog Ranch Rescue to relocate 475 beagles as Wisconsin breeding facility closes permanently
cards.teaser: Big Dog Ranch Rescue has reached an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms and transfer the remaining 475 beagles to its Florida and Alabama campuses.
cards.body:
Big Dog Ranch Rescue has reached an agreement to permanently close Ridglan Farms, a Wisconsin-based dog breeding and research facility, and transfer the remaining 475 beagles housed there. A total of 325 beagles will be transferred from Ridglan Farms to Big Dog Ranch Rescue today and tomorrow. The dogs will be transported to the organization's Florida and Alabama campuses, where they will receive medical care, including spay and neuter procedures, before being placed for adoption. Some of the beagles will also be transferred to partner rescue organizations across the country. The remaining 150 dogs are expected to be released to Big Dog Ranch Rescue by the beginning of August, at which point Ridglan Farms will permanently cease its dog breeding, sales, research and testing operations.

Lauree Simmons, founder and CEO of Big Dog Ranch Rescue, thanked Ridglan Farms for coordinating the transfers and committing to permanently close its operations. Simmons asked that the public refrain from further protests directed at Ridglan Farms, its owners, or its employees, stating that the focus should be on supporting the dogs as they transition into their new lives. The agreement follows a large-scale rescue effort carried out on April 29 that resulted in the relocation of 2,110 beagles from the facility. Founded in 2008, Big Dog Ranch Rescue has rescued more than 90,000 dogs. Those interested in adopting one of the rescued beagles or supporting transportation and medical care efforts can visit Big Dog Ranch Rescue's website for more information.

hero.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast uses Stuart thrift stores to care for cats during Palm City shelter renovation
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two Stuart thrift stores to keep animal care going during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
hero.body:
The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to store locations, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats at both thrift stores located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted, adding that donations of gently used goods are welcome. The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers hands-on ocean ecosystems exploration
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce. Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility has displayed fully live, complex models of ecosystems since 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV, noting that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms.

The exhibit's touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran said visitors will likely touch animals they've never seen before. The facility also features a barracuda that measures just four inches. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced by live displays. The facility is open to the public year-round. More information is available at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library System launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to Unearth a Story this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31, under the theme "Unearth a Story." Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen told WPTV the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

The program offers age-specific incentive prizes. Children up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck, while kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events ranging from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library offers free STREAM summer programs with daily lunches for youth
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library is making summer brighter for kids and teens with free STREAM programs in science, technology, reading, art, engineering and math, open to all Florida residents.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body

The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM summer programs for kids and teens of all ages, open to all Florida residents. STREAM stands for Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math. Located at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue in downtown Delray Beach, the library has served the community since 1913, when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection. Today it welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually to its 36,000-square-foot facility.

Young adult librarian Natalie Baron is leading programs including ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also participate in lab-based activities with collaborative 3D puzzle builds and take-home themed book boxes. Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, launched the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, which encourages young readers to set goals with librarians and track progress. Participants receive an Unearth a Story bag containing a free STREAM book and related activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library provides free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to youth up to age 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children ages 5 and older to explore STREAM topics together. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

hero.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier sues TikTok over violations of Florida child social media law
hero.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against TikTok on Monday, alleging the social media platform is violating a 2024 Florida law designed to protect minors online and deceiving parents about the content children access. The complaint centers on House Bill 3, which took effect in January and prohibits children under 14 from creating social media accounts while requiring parental consent for users ages 15 and 16.

Uthmeier stated that TikTok's business model depends on addicting children and teenagers to its platform while knowingly misleading parents. "TikTok knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law," the attorney general said. The lawsuit contends that TikTok misrepresents the types of content available on the platform, downplaying the prevalence of mature themes such as sexual content, drug use, profanity, self-harm and eating disorders despite marketing the app as appropriate for users 13 and older.

Beyond the alleged violations of HB 3, Florida's complaint charges TikTok with engaging in deceptive and unfair trade practices under the state's consumer protection laws by misleading parents about platform safety and content moderation. State attorneys argue that TikTok has long understood the risks its platform poses to young users but continues pursuing growth strategies that target children and teenagers rather than addressing these concerns.

The lawsuit represents a significant enforcement action under Florida's social media law since its implementation earlier this year. The legal challenge reflects a broader national trend of states taking action against social media companies over youth safety concerns. The outcome could establish important precedent for how other states enforce similar restrictions and determine the extent to which social media companies may face liability for allowing underage users or exposing them to inappropriate material. TikTok has not yet responded to the allegations filed in Florida court.

cards.headline: Tampa Mayor Castor warns property tax amendment could force cuts to police and fire departments
cards.teaser: Mayor Jane Castor said a proposed constitutional amendment raising the homestead exemption could cut at least $35 million from city revenue in 2028 and force painful decisions on public safety staffing.
cards.body:
Tampa Mayor Jane Castor is warning voters that a proposed constitutional amendment raising the homestead property tax exemption could force the city into painful budget choices affecting first responders. The amendment, approved by state lawmakers for the November ballot, would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It requires approval from 60% of voters to take effect. Castor said property taxes brought in $380 million for Tampa's 2026 budget but argues that amount does not cover the city's police and fire budgets as they currently stand.

Castor estimated the amendment would cut at least $35 million in city property tax revenue in 2028 and at least $60 million in 2029. She noted that Tampa has added more than 100 firefighters and 60 police officers since 2019, with crime down more than 20% over that span, arguing those gains are connected to staffing levels. "Public safety isn't optional," Castor said. She raised concerns about whether the city would have to cut recreation programs or charge businesses and tax-exempt property owners public safety fees to avoid service reductions. Tampa joins a growing list of local governments warning of potential fallout from the state's property tax push.

cards.headline: Charlie Crist joins Rick Scott in calling for cancellation of Ye concerts at Raymond James Stadium
cards.teaser: The former Governor and current St. Petersburg mayoral candidate appeared alongside Senator Rick Scott and Attorney General Ashley Moody at the Florida Holocaust Museum to demand Tampa officials cancel two June concerts over the artist's antisemitic remarks.
cards.body:
Charlie Crist joined the bipartisan push to cancel Ye's upcoming concerts at Raymond James Stadium, appearing at a news conference at the Florida Holocaust Museum alongside U.S. Senator Rick Scott, Attorney General Ashley Moody, Jewish community leaders and other officials. Crist, a former Governor and current St. Petersburg mayoral candidate, called for the Tampa Sports Authority to block the shows scheduled for June 26 and June 28. "This is right versus wrong," Crist said. "My friend, Rick, is right. We need to stand up and be there to stand up for what is right, what is fundamentally true, and what we know is evil and wrong."

Scott previously sent a letter to the Tampa Sports Authority Board of Directors urging members not to "platform a hateful person pushing evil ideologies" using taxpayer money and called Ye's antisemitic comments "an affront to the values of the people of the Hillsborough community." Scott also cited a 2025 Super Bowl ad directing viewers to merchandise featuring swastikas. Tampa Bay NOW has also called for cancellation. Tampa Sports Authority Chair Patrick Manteiga warned that canceling the contract based only on objections to Ye's past statements could expose the authority to legal risk, noting they are "probably close to selling out 100,000 tickets." The concerts remain scheduled for later this month.

cards.headline: Johnson & Johnson commits $1 billion expansion to Jacksonville Vision Manufacturing facility
cards.teaser: The healthcare giant will upgrade its Southside Jacksonville facility with advanced manufacturing and a new distribution center, with officials expecting full operation by 2028.
cards.body:
Johnson & Johnson announced it will invest $1 billion to expand its Vision Manufacturing facility on Jacksonville's Southside. The funding will support construction of an upgraded distribution facility and expanded manufacturing and packaging technologies to meet growing demand for eye healthcare products serving an estimated 40 million patients in the U.S. and worldwide. The Jacksonville factory primarily produces contact lens technology.

Chair and CEO Joaquin Duato said the investment reflects the company's conviction that advanced manufacturing in the United States is essential to delivering innovative healthcare solutions to patients. The expansion will strengthen the U.S. supply chain while helping more people with eye health needs. Company officials expect the new distribution facility to be fully operational in 2028. Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan called the investment a strong vote of confidence in Jacksonville's workforce and future. Johnson & Johnson officials noted the Jacksonville project is part of a larger $55 billion company commitment to U.S. operations through 2029 to improve manufacturing, research and technology. The company estimates it has a $6 billion annual economic impact in Florida with approximately 3,500 employees in the Jacksonville area.

cards.headline: Florida Medicaid and CHIP enrollment dips below pre-pandemic levels for first time
cards.teaser: Combined enrollment fell to 3.58 million as of February 2026, down from 3.60 million in February 2020, with child enrollment declining by roughly 107,000 over the six-year period.
cards.body:
Florida's combined Medicaid and Children's Health Insurance Program enrollment has dipped slightly below pre-pandemic levels for the first time, according to February 2026 data compiled by KFF. The latest figures show 3.58 million Floridians enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP as of February, down from 3.60 million in February 2020. Florida is among a minority of states where combined enrollment has fallen below the February 2020 baseline, while national Medicaid and CHIP enrollment remains 5% above pre-pandemic levels. KFF's Medicaid Enrollment and Unwinding Tracker shows Florida had 5.09 million people enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP in March 2023, but Florida's Medicaid caseload crested at 5.58 million in the 2022-23 fiscal year, according to the Social Services Estimating Conference.

Child enrollment in Medicaid and CHIP fell from 2.41 million in February 2020 to 2.30 million in February 2026, a decline of roughly 107,000 children, or 4%. Adult enrollment is at 1.28 million, up from 1.19 million before the pandemic, an increase of about 87,000 adults, or 7%. The most significant decline occurred within CHIP, where enrollment dropped from 240,730 children six years ago to 165,278 in February, a decrease of 31%. Medicaid enrollment alone remains slightly above pre-pandemic levels, with 3.41 million in February 2026, up from 3.36 million six years earlier. The CHIP drop comes amid the state's ongoing dispute over a federal rule requiring 12 months of continuous eligibility for children enrolled in the program, which has delayed implementation of a 2023 law expected to expand eligibility to about 40,000 children.

cards.headline: St. Cloud Representative Paula Stark exploring legal challenge after disqualification from HD 47 ballot
cards.teaser: The two-term Republican said election officials disqualified her over financial disclosure paperwork she claims was already accepted electronically the day before the qualifying deadline.
cards.body:
Paula Stark said she is working on a legal challenge after she was disqualified as a candidate for re-election to House District 47. In a new statement, the St. Cloud Republican said election officials knocked her off the ballot over a failure to file financial disclosures that had already been accepted electronically a day beforehand. Stark said the state should have already had a copy of her Form 6 disclosure, noting that the previous day her form had been filed electronically through the Commission of Ethics portal and she has the digitally accepted receipt available online. She also alleged that a disruption at the Division of Elections office on Friday, the deadline for qualifying for state office, may have impacted other candidates. "At the time we were submitting the required documents to the Division of Elections counter, they were in the process of having security remove an individual that was causing disruption of the process and had backed up close to a dozen other candidates who were in line," Stark said.

The Division of Elections shows Stark submitted much of her final paperwork in the last hour before it was due on Friday. A partisan candidate oath was received at 11:35 a.m., while a check for the amount of her qualifying fee was timestamped at 11:37 a.m. The Division of Elections shifted her status to did not qualify shortly after the deadline. The only candidates to qualify for House District 47 were Democrat Jorge Figueroa, President of the Puerto Rican Chamber of Commerce of Central Florida, and Republican Anthony Nieves, a former state investigator. Should those two remain the only candidates, a Primary on August 18 will be open to all voters in the district and decide the Representative for the next two years, meaning a pickup for Democrats in the House.

cards.headline: Democratic entrepreneur Richard Lamondin leads SD 38 fundraising with $300,000 haul including self-loans
cards.teaser: Lamondin raised more than $300,000 in the April to May period, though $100,000 came from self-loans and $30,000 from a closed federal campaign account, while incumbent Republican Senator Calatayud took in nearly $176,000.
cards.body:
Democratic entrepreneur Richard Lamondin led the Senate District 38 field in fundraising during the April 1 to May 31 period, collecting more than $300,000. However, that total included $100,000 in self-loans and a $30,000 transfer from his closed federal campaign account. In terms of new dollars entering campaigns, incumbent Republican Sen. Calatayud raised more, though most came from corporations and political committees rather than individuals. No-party candidate Jeffrey Solomon raised $9,000, including $2,000 in self-loans.

Calatayud collected nearly $176,000 between her campaign account and political committee Vision Integrity for Florida, receiving 101 contributions with 20 from personal checks. Her largest single contribution came from the political committee of St. Johns County Representative Tom Leek, a $25,000 check. The real estate industry donated $20,000 from five companies under Miami Beach-based Redwood RE Management, plus contributions from Post Real Estate Group and Associated Builders and Contractors. Calatayud spent nearly $89,000 and entered June with $1.33 million remaining. Lamondin received 227 outside contributions, just two from political or corporate sources, and had close to $283,000 by month's end. Solomon took 19 contributions and spent just over $2,800, leaving him with $6,400 by June 1. Senate District 38 covers coastal Miami-Dade municipalities including Cutler Bay, Palmetto Bay, Pinecrest and South Miami.

hero.headline: Martin County Could Lose $67 Million Under Proposed Homestead Exemption Expansion
hero.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could cost Martin County more than $67 million in lost revenue if voters approve the amendment in November, according to analysis from the Florida Policy Institute. The statewide impact would be even more significant, with local governments across Florida potentially losing nearly $4.8 billion under the measure.

The expansion raises concerns about who will ultimately bear the financial burden. Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, says the proposed tax cut would do little for the people his organization serves. He reports seeing an uptick in people seeking help with rent and bills, with 95 percent of those seeking assistance being renters. "The housing situation is so dire," Readling said. "It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday." According to a 2025 Florida Senate analysis, there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters in the state. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said.

Attorney John Tolley explains that local governments facing revenue shortfalls have limited options: cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. If rates rise, landlords who don't receive the homestead exemption could face higher tax bills and potentially pass those costs on to renters. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged this possibility, saying "There could be an effect where we see some people getting priced out of these rentals, which are already pretty high." However, Caputo believes there is a high probability that local municipalities may not raise millage rates at all. He also noted that if landlords do face higher costs, the market may stabilize anyway due to supply and demand dynamics.

The amendment includes another provision that could help offset concerns about rising rents. It would lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10 percent down to 5 percent. Tolley suggested this reduction could potentially lead to lower rents. "The fact that you could have less taxes, you actually might see a trend where rents go down even further than they were before," Tolley said. Caputo added that while landlords may initially try to pass increased costs to tenants, they would have to readjust pricing if demand doesn't support higher rents, since "costs are pretty movable as well."

cards.headline: Palm City Brush Fire Over 100 Acres Now Fully Contained
cards.teaser: A brush fire that briefly slowed traffic on Interstate 95 northbound in Palm City has been fully contained by the Florida Forest Service.
cards.body:
The Florida Forest Service contained a brush fire in Palm City that burned over 100 acres, according to reports from Monday. The fire briefly slowed traffic on Interstate 95 northbound.

The blaze is now 100% contained. No additional details about the cause of the fire or property damage were immediately available.

cards.headline: Driver Found Dead in Burning Vehicle in Martin County
cards.teaser: Charred remains were found inside a truck after a fire in Martin County. An investigation is ongoing.
cards.body:
A driver was found dead inside a burning vehicle in Martin County on Monday, according to reports. The charred remains were discovered inside a truck after a mysterious fire.

Authorities are investigating the incident. The cause of the fire and the identity of the driver have not been released.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Leaders to Decide How to Spend $24 Million Waste Pro Settlement
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie city council will discuss what to do with the $24 million received as part of a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders are discussing what to do with the $24 million they received as part of a settlement with their former trash hauler Waste Pro. In 2021, both the company and city filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued it was a breach of contract for the standard of service. cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens Woman Receives Repeated Toll Bills Tied to Stolen Temp Tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens has been receiving toll bills for roads she and her husband have never traveled, linked to a temporary tag registered to her husband.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens went to her mailbox in March and found a toll bill for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast. The license plate number on the bill matched a temporary tag registered to her husband. The bill referenced a black Mercedes and included a picture of it. The Keswicks drive a white Nissan, which has had a permanent tag for months. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police. She said the situation quickly became more concerning than a bill for under $10. "The guy runs a red light, the tag is in my husband's name. The guy hits and runs, tag is under my husband's name," she said.

Following police advice, Keswick-Paine did not pay the bill and instead filed a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived anyway. SunPass eventually closed the dispute, but Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation that the matter was resolved. Since reaching out in April and submitting two monthly toll bills and subsequent disputes, she received a third toll bill. Palm Beach Gardens Police said in an email that they consider the case an isolated incident, but personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said the problem is far more common. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino said the best way to protect yourself from temp tag theft is to keep thorough records of any police reports and toll disputes.

hero.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million loss from proposed property tax amendment
hero.body:
Indian River County leaders are warning that a proposed property tax amendment could cost the county $50 million in revenue. The warning comes as voters prepare to decide on the amendment in November.

A recent analysis from the Florida Policy Institute estimates that local governments statewide could lose nearly $4.8 billion if voters approve the amendment. The proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption would lower tax bills for homeowners but could force local governments to cut services, use reserves, or raise millage rates to offset the lost revenue.

Critics warn that renters may end up bearing the burden if local governments raise rates. At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling says 95% of the people seeking help with rent and bills are renters. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10% down to 5%. Some analysts believe this could result in lower rents, though others warn landlords facing higher tax bills could pass those costs to tenants. The measure will appear on the November ballot.

On Saturday just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle. The individual was burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire, but after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives believe they have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed. Those results are expected to take several weeks.
